name: Jamal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Harbourline Foods, a distributor that supplies school canteens and care homes with frozen and dry goods. I'm in by 7:30, and the first hour is the overnight price emails from suppliers, which I read on paper because I think better that way. Then I'm on the phone to the rice importer, the frozen veg people, the poultry contract. By mid-afternoon I'm checking stock levels against what the canteens ordered for the term.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the relationships. The man who sells us chickpeas has known me fifteen years, and he rings me first when a ship is late. What wears me out is the squeeze: every year the buyers carry more suppliers and the pay stays flat. My wife Lena is a nurse, my kids are Mia and Theo, and the mortgage on our terrace off Canal Road eats most of two salaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd shrug. Software has been promising to do my job since I started, and so far it's mainly given me more screens to check. I'd say at work that we'll see a few reminders and reports done faster, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not relaxed even if it's hype. We have under a month of savings, my pay is lower than buyers get elsewhere, and there are very few similar jobs round here. If Harbourline had a bad year, I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd keep the supplier calls, keep checking prices myself, and ask Lena to keep her extra shifts at the hospital. I'd try to put a little aside each month, maybe a hundred, towards a proper cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing still on a moving walkway. Nothing new arrives, but the bills do. I'm tired more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you read the price emails on paper. What would you do if the routine bits got automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something went wrong at Harbourline, we'd cut the kids' swimming and the holiday first. Then the car insurance gets shopped around. The mortgage is the one thing we'd never touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You carry a lot already. What's the first thing that gets squeezed if work gets harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last time the supplier's system was down for two days, I worked off my paper notes and we didn't miss a delivery. That's why I trust the paper. If the routine software gets slightly better, good, but I won't be the first to switch.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **routine** tasks get quicker, but nothing big moves.
I'd say software has promised a lot before, and my **paper notes** still saved us in an outage.
think: I'm still worried because we have **under a month** saved and few buyer jobs nearby.
A bad year at Harbourline would hit us hard, whatever AI does.
do: Keep calling suppliers and **checking prices** myself.
Put aside about **a hundred a month** towards a real cushion.
Ask Lena to keep her extra hospital shifts.
feel: **Tired** more than scared; the bills keep arriving whether or not AI changes anything.
S0.quote: Last time the supplier's system was down for two days, I worked off my paper notes and we didn't miss a delivery.
fieldNote: Jamal's worry here is **money**, not technology: thin savings, lower pay, few local jobs.
He sounds relaxed about AI itself, which shows his habit of trusting the familiar.
Lena's shifts are the household's real safety net.

steps.text: Keep placing supplier orders by phone and checking prices on paper
Move a hundred a month into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need proper rules before anyone is replaced. I'd want a written agreement that automated buying doesn't mean fewer buyers by the back door. As union rep for the office staff I'd push that in the first meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'd keep two buyers where there are five now. The price comparison and reordering is exactly what a program can do. I'm among the best, but being best at something a machine does cheaply doesn't protect you for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get on the union's retraining list and ask Harbourline to put me on any pilot early, so I'm not the man they push out. I'd learn the tool at home on a weekend and not tell anyone how clumsy I am at first. Lena would add hours, and we'd stop the kids' clubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair, honestly. I spent twenty years learning which suppliers cheat on weights, and a machine gets that for free. I also feel angry at the owners, who'll bank the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on the card's list of tasks AI takes first. What does that look like at Harbourline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a buyer tells me to try a tool, I'll try it, but I want to see it work on my own orders first. I'd test it on the care-home account, which is small, where a mistake won't hurt anyone. I won't trust a tool with the school canteens until I've checked it a hundred times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. What would it take for you to try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not afraid of the machine, I'm afraid of the meeting where they say it's saved twenty percent and who goes. In that meeting I'd want the union beside me, because alone I'd be the quiet one.

say: I'd demand a written deal that **automated buying** doesn't quietly mean fewer buyers.
As union rep I'd push for **retraining** before any cuts.
think: I expect Harbourline to keep **two buyers** where there are five now.
Being the best at a task a machine does cheaply won't protect me for long.
do: Join the union **retraining list** and ask for an early place on any pilot.
Learn the tool at home on **weekends**, starting with the small care-home account.
Ask Lena for extra hospital hours and drop the kids' clubs.
feel: **Angry** that owners will bank the savings from my twenty years of knowledge.
Uneasy about being clumsy with a tool in front of colleagues.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of the machine, I'm afraid of the meeting where they say it's saved twenty percent and who goes.
fieldNote: He expects the buying team to shrink and thinks he might be on the list despite seniority.
His **union role** is both his shield and his plan.
Pride in supplier knowledge turns into anger at owners.

steps.text: Push the union for a written no-cuts deal on automated buying
Sign up for the union's retraining list this winter
Test a buying tool on the small care-home account first
Drop the kids' swimming and clubs to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this can't be left to the market, and I'd say it loud: governments need to step in with income support and rules for firms. Online I'd probably write something angry and then delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it means my job goes, probably within the two years, because buying is almost pure thinking work. Lena's hospital job is safer since hands-on care comes later, and I'd be glad of that. But one nurse's wage doesn't cover a mortgage and two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd try to get a redundancy deal through the union before the firm gets ahead of us. I'd put every spare pound against the mortgage and stop all extras. I'd also look at warehouse and delivery supervision jobs, where hands still matter for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared, and I'd be ashamed that I'm scared. I'd lie awake adding up months. With less than a month saved, I know the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do on day one, and what do you tell Mia and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mia and Theo that Dad's work is changing, that we'll be fine, and that the house stays. I wouldn't tell them about the savings. Mia is eleven and she notices, so I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You work in thinking-heavy work, and robots come later. Does that give you or your household anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delay for robots helps Lena more than me. Maybe I could move to the floor of the warehouse for a few years, but that's a big drop in status and in pay. I'd take it if it kept the mortgage paid.

say: I'd say **governments** must step in with income support and rules for firms.
I'd post something angry online, then probably delete it.
think: My **job goes** within two years, because buying is almost all thinking work.
Lena's nursing job is safer, but one wage won't carry the **mortgage**.
do: Press the union for a **redundancy deal** before the firm gets ahead of us.
Put every spare pound against the **mortgage** and stop extras.
Look at warehouse and delivery supervisor jobs where hands still matter.
feel: **Scared**, and ashamed of being scared, lying awake adding up months.
Relieved only that Lena's work is safer for a while.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake adding up months. With less than a month saved, I know the sums.
fieldNote: Jamal takes the **two-year** card at face value and expects to lose his job.
He sees the robot delay as Lena's protection, not his.
Considers a status drop to warehouse work and would accept it.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain a redundancy deal before the firm moves
Put every spare pound against the mortgage
Apply for warehouse and delivery supervisor jobs at nearby depots
Vote and campaign for income support for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people act now, so I'd tell colleagues to get organised early. I'd ask the union to start a joint panel with management on how buying work will change. Online I'd probably share articles on public retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the same ending, just with a longer wait to be afraid. Buying goes. I'd rather have the time, but I know I'm slow, and time isn't help if I spend it avoiding the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start learning one AI tool seriously, even though I hate it. I'd enrol in an evening course, maybe supply chain planning or something I can hold up as hands-on-adjacent. I'd also push the mortgage down with a part-time weekend job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long wait at a bus stop where I know the bus isn't coming. There's some relief in the time, but it also drags on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives a bit more room. What would you actually do in year one that you couldn't do in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Mia is sixteen and Theo is thirteen when it lands. I'd want to have the mortgage nearly gone by then. Lena could finish the nursing management course she keeps putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the time change for Lena and the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids can see it coming with me. I'd talk about it properly and show them how a budget works. I'd rather they know the truth than hear it from a school friend.

say: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough if we **organise early**.
I'd ask the union for a joint panel with management on buying work.
think: It's the same ending as the faster story, with a longer wait to be **afraid**.
I'm slow with new tools and could waste the time **avoiding** them.
do: Learn one **AI tool** properly, even though I dislike it.
Take an evening course in **supply chain planning**.
Work a weekend job to push the mortgage down.
feel: Like a **long wait** at a bus stop, with some relief and some drag.
S3.quote: I think it's the same ending, just with a longer wait to be afraid.
fieldNote: Extra time helps his plans, but he is honest that he **avoids** new things.
He turns to family planning: Lena's course, the kids' ages.
Mood stays high because his own job still goes.

steps.text: Learn one AI buying tool at home, starting this winter
Enrol in an evening course in supply chain planning
Take a weekend warehouse job to pay the mortgage down
Help Lena finish her nursing management course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say that's long enough to do this fairly, and I'd stay on the union's case about it. At the pub with friends I'd say my kids' generation will have it worst, so we should fix schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be cautiously okay. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage should be paid off, and the kids nearly grown. I'd still worry about the job going, but I'd have time to move sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well for now and put money away every month, aiming for six months of cover in three years. I'd take on a couple of the new software tools slowly, one a year. I'd also ask Harbourline about a supervisor path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, which surprises me. The calm comes from time, not from trust in anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is it still a worry, or does it become a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms and the governments. Firms will always pick the cheapest option, so governments have to set the rules and pay for retraining. I'd vote for whoever promises that, even if I disagreed with them on other things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for how this turns out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan, mostly. Ten years lets me build a cushion before the change, and the cushion is what I've never had. The worry is the next few years, because the pay and mortgage pressure don't wait.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to do this **fairly** if unions stay involved.
I'd tell friends our kids' generation needs **better schools**.
think: By 2036 I'd be fifty-three with the mortgage **nearly paid**, so I'd be cautiously okay.
I still worry about the next few years of **tight money**.
do: Build a **six-month cushion** within three years.
Pick up one new software tool a year, slowly.
feel: **Manageable**, which surprises me; the calm comes from time, not trust.
S4.quote: The calm comes from time, not from trust in anyone.
fieldNote: Ten years turns dread into a **plan** for him.
He blames firms and governments, in line with his union, left-leaning outlook.
His current money squeeze keeps him anxious even here.

steps.text: Build a six-month savings cushion within three years
Learn one new buying software tool each year
Ask Harbourline about moving into a team supervisor role
Vote for parties promising paid retraining for displaced workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. I'd have no time to build any cushion, and the mortgage doesn't care about timing. What would help is a firm redundancy agreement through the union, paid retraining that doesn't wipe out our income, and some help with mortgage payments for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get lumped in with those who ignore change. I don't ignore it. I just want it to be fair, and I want to see it work before I stake my family's house on it.

headlineQuote: I don't ignore it. I just want it to be fair, and I want to see it work before I stake my family's house on it.
portrait: Jamal Zhang, 43, is a senior **wholesale buyer** at a food distributor supplying school canteens and care homes.
He's a union rep, left-leaning, and trusts paper and phone relationships over software; he **never uses AI**.
With under a month saved, a mortgage and few similar jobs, he is anxious even if AI fizzles.
He expects buying work to go in fast scenarios and leans on the **union**, Lena's nursing job and slow learning.
Ten years turns dread into a plan; two years leaves him scared.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, with no time to build any savings against the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A firm **redundancy agreement** through the union, paid retraining and a year of mortgage help.
